question: What's the difference between costume design and fashion design, and why does that distinction matter to you?
lookingFor: Understanding that costume serves character and story rather than personal style or trend, plus a genuine reason the applicant is drawn to costume specifically.

bullets: Explain costume design serves a character, script, and story rather than the wearer's personal taste
Contrast with fashion design, which is often about trend, brand identity, or self-expression
Give a personal reason why storytelling through clothing is what pulls you in
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Fashion design is usually about creating something that reflects a brand or a trend and that the wearer chooses for themselves. Costume design starts from a completely different place, because you're not asking what looks good, you're asking what this character would actually put on and why. I got interested in that difference doing a school play where I redesigned a hand-me-down jacket to look decades older for a grandfather character, and realized the clothes could tell the audience who he was before he said a word. That's the part of design I want to spend my career doing.

commonMistakes: Treating costume design as just 'fashion for movies'
Focusing on trends or personal style rather than character
Giving no concrete example connecting the two ideas
followUps: Can you think of a costume that would look great on a hanger but wrong on screen?

question: Why do you want to study costume design at our university specifically?
lookingFor: Specific, researched motivation tied to this course's facilities, staff, or curriculum, not generic praise.

bullets: Name a specific studio, workshop, module, or tutor's work you researched
Connect it to a concrete personal experience or gap in your current skills
Show you understand what makes this course distinct from others you could apply to
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I looked closely at your course because it has a dedicated construction workshop alongside the design studio, and I've realized through school productions that I can sketch a strong idea but my pattern cutting is still shaky. I also read about the second-year placement with a regional theatre, which is exactly the kind of practical exposure I haven't had access to yet. Most fashion-adjacent courses I looked at were much more product and trend focused, and yours is one of the few built specifically around narrative and character work.

commonMistakes: Praise that would apply to any design course
Citing rankings or reputation instead of course content
Not knowing what makes this course different from a fashion degree
followUps: What skill are you hoping this course will help you build that you don't have yet?

question: What first drew you to costume design?
lookingFor: A genuine, specific origin story that shows early and sustained engagement with the field.

bullets: Point to a specific moment, production, or object, not a vague love of clothes
Show the interest has continued and grown, not a one-off memory
Tie it back to what excites you about costume specifically
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I was in the wardrobe crew for my school's production of a period drama, and I remember dressing an actor in a corset and watching how differently she stood and moved once it was on. That was the moment I realized clothes weren't just decoration, they were doing real work on the performance. Since then I've volunteered on three more school and community shows, and I always ask to help with costume rather than set or lighting.

commonMistakes: A generic 'I've always loved fashion' with no specific memory
An interest that sounds recent or untested
Confusing enjoying clothes with understanding costume's function
followUps: Has your understanding of costume design changed since that first experience?

question: Tell us about a costume from a film, show, or play that you think is particularly well designed, and explain why.
lookingFor: An analytical eye that can articulate how a specific costume choice serves character, story, or period, beyond just liking it.

bullets: Name a specific costume, not a whole show's general look
Explain what the costume communicates about the character or moment
Note a specific design choice, silhouette, color, or fabric, that does the work
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I keep coming back to the gradual change in Cersei's costumes across Game of Thrones, especially how the necklines and armor plating creep in as she loses allies and starts building her own power. By the final seasons she's wearing structured black with metal detailing that reads almost like armor, even in scenes with no fighting. It's such a clear example of costume tracking a character arc without a line of dialogue announcing it, and it made me pay much closer attention to how designers use small shifts over a whole series rather than one big reveal.

commonMistakes: Naming a whole show's aesthetic instead of a specific costume choice
Only describing what it looks like, not what it communicates
Picking an example that suggests limited or narrow viewing
followUps: Would that costume choice work as well on stage as it does on screen?

question: Talk us through one piece in your portfolio, from initial idea to final result.
lookingFor: Ability to explain a full design process clearly and take ownership of decisions, including what didn't work.

bullets: Start from the brief or character, not straight to the finished image
Explain a key decision and why you made it, including any research behind it
Be honest about a change you made along the way or something you'd revise
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The piece I'd start with is a redesign I did of a costume for Lady Macbeth set in a 1920s context instead of the original period. I researched how women's silhouettes shifted after the first World War, since I wanted her ambition to read as modern and restrictive at the same time, so I chose a dropped waist gown but kept it in a heavy dark fabric that moves stiffly rather than the loose flowing styles typical of the era. My first sketch had her in red, but I switched to a deep green because red felt too obvious for her guilt arc, and I wanted something that could shift meaning as the lighting changed across acts. Looking back I'd probably push the silhouette further from period accuracy to make the concept even bolder.

commonMistakes: Describing only the finished look with no process
Refusing to admit any weakness or change in the work
Using jargon without explaining the reasoning in plain terms
followUps: What would you change if you had more time or budget for that piece?

question: When you're given a script, how do you begin turning a character into a costume?
lookingFor: A clear, structured design process starting from character and text before moving to visual research.

bullets: Start with a close reading of the text for clues about the character
Move to research, period, setting, social status, before sketching
Mention checking choices against the director's overall vision
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I start by reading the script at least twice, once for story and once specifically hunting for clues, what a character says about their own clothes, what others say about them, and any stage directions about movement or changing. Then I build a small research board around their world, period, class, climate, occupation, before I let myself sketch anything, because I don't want my first instinct to just be what looks cool. Once I have a rough direction I try to check it against what the director has said about tone, since a costume that's technically accurate but tonally wrong for the production doesn't actually work.

commonMistakes: Jumping straight to sketching without textual or historical research
Designing in isolation from the director's or production's overall vision
Treating every character as a blank slate with no attention to what the script actually says
followUps: What do you do if the director's vision conflicts with what you think the character needs?

question: Can you explain what a costume plot is and why it's used?
lookingFor: Working knowledge of production terminology and the practical, organizational side of costume design, not just the creative side.

bullets: Define it as a scene-by-scene or character-by-character breakdown of every costume and change
Explain it's used for tracking quick changes, continuity, and budgeting
Show awareness it's a practical tool shared with the wardrobe team, not just the designer
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A costume plot is essentially a chart that maps out every character against every scene, showing exactly what they're wearing and when a change happens. I first had to make one for a school production with a lot of doubling, actors playing two roles, and it was the only way to catch that one actor needed a full change in under ninety seconds between scenes. It's really a communication tool as much as a planning one, because the wardrobe supervisor, dressers, and stage manager all need to work from the same document to keep quick changes running smoothly.

commonMistakes: Confusing a costume plot with a mood board or research board
Describing it only as a creative document with no practical function
Being unable to explain who actually uses it during a production
followUps: How would a costume plot change between a film shoot and a live stage run?

question: How would you go about researching a costume for a play set in a specific historical period you don't know well?
lookingFor: A concrete, credible research method that goes beyond a quick internet image search.

bullets: Mention primary sources: paintings, photographs, surviving garments, museum collections
Show awareness that not everything needs to be literally accurate, some choices serve the story over strict accuracy
Note checking things like undergarments and construction, not just the visible silhouette
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd start with primary sources rather than other people's costume designs, so paintings and photographs from the actual period, and if possible museum collections or archives that have real surviving garments. I'd also look at what's underneath the visible layer, corsetry, petticoats, tailoring, because those shape how the outer garment sits and moves and get missed if you only look at portraits. That said, I'd hold the historical accuracy loosely where it conflicts with the story, since the goal is a believable world for this production, not a museum reconstruction.

commonMistakes: Relying only on other costume dramas as research rather than primary sources
Ignoring underlayers and structure that shape how period silhouettes actually sit
Treating historical accuracy as more important than serving the story
followUps: Can you think of a time a costume drama got a small period detail wrong, and did it matter?

question: What's different about designing a costume for the stage compared to designing for film or television?
lookingFor: Understanding of how distance, lighting, camera, and repetition change practical and design decisions between mediums.

bullets: Note that stage costumes are read from a distance and need bolder shapes, colors, or detail
Note that screen costumes are seen in close-up, so texture and small detail matter more, and continuity across takes is critical
Mention durability differences, stage costumes survive many repeat performances, screen costumes may need multiples for one scene
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: On stage the audience is often thirty or more feet away and under strong lighting, so detail gets lost and you have to design with bolder silhouettes, saturated color, or exaggerated texture so the shape still reads from the back row. On screen the camera can be inches from an actor's face, so a seam that's slightly off or fabric that looks cheap in close-up will be very obvious, and continuity matters enormously because a scene gets shot out of order across multiple days. I also think about durability differently, a stage costume needs to survive eight shows a week, while a film costume might need three or four identical copies for one scene alone, for stunts, wear, and backup.

commonMistakes: Assuming the same costume choices work identically in both mediums
Ignoring continuity requirements specific to film and TV shoots
Not knowing that multiples of a costume are often needed for screen work
followUps: Why might a screen costume need several identical copies made?

question: How can color be used in costume design to say something about a character?
lookingFor: Basic grasp of color as a storytelling tool, with a specific example rather than vague statements.

bullets: Explain color can signal mood, allegiance, status, or change over time
Give a specific example of a color choice and what it communicates
Show awareness that meaning is contextual, not fixed across every story
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Color is one of the fastest ways to tell an audience something before a character even speaks, since we read warm and cool tones, brightness, and saturation almost instinctively. In a project I worked on I dressed a character in bright yellow early on to set her apart as hopeful and a little naive, then slowly muted that yellow into greys as the story got darker for her. What I've learned though is that color meaning isn't fixed, red can mean danger, passion, or power depending on everything else around it, so I try to build the meaning specifically for that story rather than relying on a universal color code.

commonMistakes: Reciting a generic color-meaning chart with no story-specific application
Claiming color meanings are universal and fixed
Giving no concrete example from real or imagined work
followUps: Would that color choice still work if the costume were seen mostly under stage lighting rather than daylight?

question: How do you decide what fabric to use for a costume, beyond just how it looks?
lookingFor: Understanding that fabric choice involves drape, movement, weight, durability, and how it reads under lighting or on camera.

bullets: Mention drape and how it moves with the actor's action, running, dancing, fighting
Consider weight and comfort for repeated wear over a long shoot or run
Note how fabric reads under specific lighting or on camera, not just in hand
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I always try to think about how the actor is actually moving in the costume, not just how the fabric looks laid flat, because a stiff heavy fabric can completely change someone's physicality if they're meant to be running or dancing. Weight matters too since an actor might be wearing it for twelve hours across a shoot day, and something that looks perfect but is unbearable to wear for that long is a real problem. I also try to test fabric under the kind of lighting it'll actually be seen in, because some fabrics that look rich in daylight go flat or shiny under stage or studio lights.

commonMistakes: Choosing fabric purely on visual appeal in a shop or online
Ignoring how the actor needs to move in the costume
Not considering how fabric will actually look under production lighting
followUps: Have you worked with a fabric that behaved very differently once it was made up than you expected?

question: What does costume continuity mean, and why is it especially important on a film set?
lookingFor: Practical understanding of how out-of-sequence filming requires careful tracking of costume details.

bullets: Explain scenes are often shot out of story order, so costumes must match exactly across shoot days
Mention tools used to track it: continuity photos, notes on damage, dirt, buttons
Show awareness of what breaks continuity: a missing accessory, a different level of wear on the same costume
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Continuity means making sure a costume looks exactly consistent with itself across a scene, even though film is almost never shot in the order the story happens in. If a character gets a rip in their sleeve in scene ten, that rip needs to be there in every later shot of that scene and absent in every earlier one, even if those are filmed weeks apart. On a student short I worked on, we took continuity photos after every take, noting things like how undone a button was or how messy the hair looked, because it's incredibly easy to lose track of small details like that when you're not filming in order.

commonMistakes: Not knowing that films are typically shot out of sequence
Describing continuity only in general terms with no practical tracking method
Underestimating how small a detail can break continuity, buttons, dirt, jewelry
followUps: What would you do if you noticed a continuity error after a scene had already wrapped?

question: How would you costume a production with a very limited budget?
lookingFor: Practical resourcefulness: prioritizing hero pieces, sourcing secondhand, and altering rather than buying everything new.

bullets: Mention prioritizing spend on hero or close-up pieces over background costumes
Discuss sourcing options: charity shops, costume hire, altering existing stock
Show willingness to build or modify rather than default to buying new
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd start by working out which costumes really matter, the leads and any costume that gets a close-up or does heavy story work, and put most of the budget there, while background and ensemble costumes can be pulled together more cheaply. For a school production with almost no budget I sourced most of our pieces from charity shops and then altered them, dyeing a plain coat and adding trim to make it read as much older and richer looking than it actually was. I'd rather spend time modifying something imperfect into exactly what's needed than spend money we don't have trying to buy the perfect piece outright.

commonMistakes: Assuming a low budget means a lower-quality result across the board
Not knowing practical sourcing options like secondhand shops or hire houses
Spending equally across every costume instead of prioritizing key pieces
followUps: What's a low-cost technique you'd use to make a plain garment look expensive?

question: What would you do if a director wanted a costume choice you strongly disagreed with as a designer?
lookingFor: Mature collaborative instinct: advocating for your view with reasoning while ultimately respecting the director's authority over the vision.

bullets: Show you'd explain your reasoning clearly rather than simply complying or refusing
Acknowledge the director holds the final creative authority on a production
Suggest a compromise or alternative rather than a flat standoff
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd want to understand why they wanted that choice first, since there's often a reason behind it I haven't considered, maybe something about blocking or a shot they have planned. Then I'd explain my own reasoning clearly, using the script or research to back it up rather than just saying it feels wrong, and offer an alternative that might solve both our concerns. At the end of the day the director is responsible for the overall vision, so if they still want their original choice after hearing me out, I'd do my best to make it work well rather than sulking about it.

commonMistakes: Refusing to compromise or treating the disagreement as a battle to win
Simply complying with no attempt to explain a professional concern
Forgetting that the director has final creative authority
followUps: Can you think of a time your first instinct on a design turned out to be wrong?

question: Can you explain what silhouette means in costume design, and give an example of how it changed across a historical period?
lookingFor: Grasp of a core costume vocabulary term plus concrete historical knowledge, not just definitional recall.

bullets: Define silhouette as the overall outline or shape a garment creates on the body
Give a specific historical example of a silhouette shift
Note what drove the change, technology, social attitudes, practicality
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Silhouette is the overall outline a costume creates when you see it from a distance, before you notice any detail, fabric, or color, just the shape. A clear example is how women's silhouettes shifted from the wide, structured hoop skirts of the mid-1800s to the much straighter, looser shapes of the 1920s. That change wasn't just a fashion whim, it followed real shifts in women's lives, more movement, more work outside the home, and less appetite for restrictive structure, and I find it fascinating that you can read social history just from watching how a silhouette narrows or widens over decades.

commonMistakes: Confusing silhouette with fabric, color, or specific garment type
Naming a historical shift with no explanation of what drove it
Giving an answer that's purely definitional with no example
followUps: Can you name another period where silhouette shifted dramatically, and why?

question: What hands-on experience do you have with garment construction or sewing?
lookingFor: Honest account of actual making experience, including limitations, showing willingness to develop technical craft skill.

bullets: Describe specific garments or projects you've actually made or altered
Be honest about your current skill level rather than overstating it
Show eagerness to build the skill further through this course
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'm mostly self-taught through my school's drama club, I've hand-sewn simple alterations, hems, taking things in, adding trim, and I built one full bodice from a commercial pattern for a friend's play, though it took me three attempts to get the fit right. I wouldn't call myself an advanced sewer yet, I still struggle with fitted tailoring and anything involving boning or structured undergarments. That's actually one of the main things I'm looking forward to in this course, getting proper training in construction rather than teaching myself from tutorials.

commonMistakes: Overstating skill level that doesn't match the described experience
Vague claims of sewing ability with no specific project named
Presenting a lack of formal training as a weakness with no plan to address it
followUps: What's a construction technique you'd most like to get properly trained in?

question: Is there a costume designer whose work you particularly admire? What draws you to it?
lookingFor: Genuine, specific knowledge of the field beyond famous titles, with reasoning tied to design craft rather than fame.

bullets: Name a specific designer, not just a film or actor they dressed
Point to specific work and what makes their design choices distinctive
Show it's shaped your own thinking, not just a name-drop
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I really admire Sandy Powell's work, particularly on Carol, because the restraint of it struck me, she uses very controlled, muted color and clean tailored lines to show two women who have to hide so much of themselves inside 1950s conventions. It's the opposite of the more obviously spectacular costume work she's known for on something like The Favourite, and I like that she clearly chooses her design language based on what each story needs rather than having one signature look. Seeing that range made me realize good costume design is really about serving the story differently every time, not building a personal brand.

commonMistakes: Naming an actor or a film title instead of an actual costume designer
General praise with no reference to specific work or technique
Choosing someone purely for fame with no real understanding of their craft
followUps: Has that designer's work influenced anything you've made yourself?

question: What is 'breaking down' or ageing a costume, and how might you achieve it?
lookingFor: Technical knowledge of distressing techniques and understanding of why realism in wear matters to storytelling.

bullets: Define breakdown as making a costume look worn, dirty, or aged to suit a character or story
Name specific techniques: sandpaper, dye, tea staining, controlled fraying
Note the importance of doing it deliberately and consistently rather than randomly
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Breaking down a costume means deliberately ageing or distressing it so it looks like it's actually been lived in, worn for years of labor, or survived something rough, rather than looking like a brand new garment straight off a rack. Techniques I've read about and tried on a small scale include sanding fabric at stress points like knees and elbows, tea or coffee staining for a dirtied, aged tone, and carefully fraying edges in a controlled way rather than just ripping randomly. The key thing I've learned is that it has to be deliberate and consistent with the character's actual story, someone who works outdoors gets worn differently than someone who's been in the same suit indoors for a week.

commonMistakes: Describing damage as random rather than deliberate and story-driven
Naming no actual technique, just the general concept
Ignoring that breakdown needs to be consistent with a character's specific circumstances
followUps: How would you make sure a breakdown effect is reversible or repeatable if you need multiples?

question: How might costume design be used to show class or social hierarchy within a group of characters?
lookingFor: Ability to think about costume across an ensemble, using fabric quality, fit, color, and accessory as class signals.

bullets: Mention fabric quality and cut as immediate class signals, tailored fit versus ill-fitting
Discuss color and dye cost historically, or brand and newness signals in modern settings
Show thinking at the ensemble level, not just individual characters in isolation
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A lot of it comes down to fit and fabric quality before anything else, a well-tailored garment that sits properly on the body reads as wealth almost instantly, while something ill-fitting or made from cheaper fabric reads as lower status even at a glance. Historically color was a real class marker too, since certain dyes were expensive and restricted, so I'd research what colors were actually accessible to different classes in that period rather than picking colors purely for how they look. I also think about it across a whole scene, not just one character, so if I'm dressing a ballroom I'm deciding who gets the newest silhouette and who's still wearing something a season or two out of date, because that contrast tells its own story.

commonMistakes: Only considering one character in isolation rather than the whole group
Relying on modern class signals without checking historical accuracy for period pieces
Reducing class signaling to price alone, ignoring fit, condition, and cut
followUps: How would you show a character rising or falling in status purely through costume across a story?

question: How does knowing a scene will be shot in close-up change how you design or finish a costume?
lookingFor: Understanding of how camera distance changes the level of finish, texture, and detail a costume needs.

bullets: Explain close-ups reveal texture, stitching, and small imperfections invisible from a distance
Note that trims, jewelry, and fabric choices need to hold up to scrutiny in close shots
Mention checking finish through an actual camera or monitor, not just by eye
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: If I know a scene is going to be a tight close-up, I have to assume every detail will be visible, stitching, fabric texture, whether a button is real or a cheap substitute, in a way that just wouldn't register on stage from thirty feet away. That means I'd spend more time on the finish of that specific piece, proper seams rather than shortcuts, real materials rather than obvious synthetics if the budget allows it, and I'd want to actually check it on a monitor or through a camera during a fitting rather than trusting how it looks in the room. It's changed how I think about where to spend limited construction time, since a background costume in a wide shot can take shortcuts that a hero costume in close-up simply can't.

commonMistakes: Treating every costume with the same level of finish regardless of shot type
Not knowing to check a costume through an actual camera or monitor
Focusing only on silhouette and ignoring small detail that close-ups expose
followUps: What kind of costume detail might look fine on stage but fall apart under camera scrutiny?

question: If you were asked to design costumes representing a culture that isn't your own, how would you approach the research?
lookingFor: Awareness that respectful, accurate representation requires deeper research and, ideally, consultation, not just visual reference gathering.

bullets: Go beyond surface visual research to understand meaning, context, and significance of garments
Mention seeking consultation from people within that culture where possible
Show awareness of the difference between respectful representation and stereotype or costume-as-cliche
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd want to go well beyond just collecting reference images, because clothing from any culture usually carries meaning I might not recognize as an outsider, certain garments, colors, or patterns can be tied to specific ceremonies, status, or regions that don't apply everywhere. Where possible I'd try to find someone from that culture to consult with, even informally, because there's a real difference between researching a culture from books alone and getting feedback from someone who's actually lived it. I'd also be careful to avoid flattening a whole culture into one generic costume look, since that's often where representation goes wrong, treating a specific tradition as an aesthetic rather than something with real context and history.

commonMistakes: Treating cultural research the same as any historical period research with no extra care
Relying only on visual references with no attempt to understand meaning or context
Not considering consultation with people from that culture
followUps: What would you do if a script's stage directions asked for something you felt was a stereotype?

question: What design or digital tools have you used, or would you like to learn, for costume design?
lookingFor: Awareness of relevant industry tools and honest account of current skill level, with enthusiasm to grow technically.

bullets: Name specific tools used or known about, sketching software, Clo3D, pattern drafting programs
Be honest about current level rather than overstating familiarity
Connect the tool to an actual design need, fit visualization, presentation, draping simulation
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: So far I've mostly worked traditionally, hand sketching and physical mood boards, but I've used Procreate on an iPad for a few digital costume renders because it let me try color variations quickly without repainting from scratch. I've read about Clo3D, which lets you simulate how fabric drapes on a virtual body before you cut anything, and I'd really like to learn it properly, since it seems incredibly useful for testing an idea before committing expensive fabric to it. I know my digital skills are still fairly basic compared to my hand sketching, and that's an area I specifically want this course to help me build.

commonMistakes: Claiming advanced software skill with no specific example to back it up
Dismissing digital tools as unnecessary for costume design
Naming a tool with no understanding of what it actually does
followUps: Why might a director or producer prefer seeing a digital render over a hand sketch?

question: How would you design a costume that needs to come off or go on in under thirty seconds during a live show?
lookingFor: Practical, technical problem-solving that balances a design vision against real backstage constraints.

bullets: Mention hidden fastenings that are fast to operate: velcro, magnets, snaps instead of many buttons
Discuss layering and pre-rigging a costume so a dresser can help swiftly
Show awareness this requires working closely with the wardrobe or stage management team
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: For anything that needs to change that fast, I'd avoid small fiddly fastenings like a full row of buttons entirely and build in something like a hidden zip, velcro, or magnetic closures that a dresser can operate by feel in the dark backstage. I'd also try to pre-rig the costume as much as possible, so a coat might be sewn to fasten in one motion even though it looks fully tailored from the audience. That kind of solution really has to come out of talking directly with the dresser doing the change and the stage manager about the actual wing space and timing, because a great idea on paper can fail completely if there's nowhere for the dresser to stand.

commonMistakes: Designing purely for visual effect with no consideration of change speed
Not knowing practical fast-fastening options beyond standard buttons or zips
Failing to mention collaborating with dressers or stage management on the logistics
followUps: What would you do if the actor themselves found the quick-change costume physically uncomfortable?

question: How does costume design need to work with the wider production or set design of a show?
lookingFor: Understanding that costume is one part of a unified visual world, requiring active collaboration with other design departments.

bullets: Explain costume needs to sit within the same visual world as set, lighting, and props
Mention practical coordination: color palettes not clashing or disappearing against set
Show this requires ongoing communication, not designing in isolation and combining at the end
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Costume can't really be designed in isolation, because an actor in a beautifully designed costume can still disappear visually if it's the same color and tone as the set behind them, or clash badly under a particular lighting design. I try to stay in contact with the set and lighting designers early on, even just sharing color palettes, so we're building one coherent world rather than three separate visions that happen to end up on the same stage. On a project I worked on, the set designer and I actually swapped mood boards before either of us finalized anything, and it meant our final color choices complemented each other instead of accidentally competing.

commonMistakes: Designing costume in isolation and only checking against the set at the last minute
Not considering how costume colors interact with lighting design
Treating costume as more important than the other departments rather than one part of a whole
followUps: What would you do if your costume colors and the set designer's palette clashed close to opening night?

question: What would you bring to a group of costume design students working on a joint production?
lookingFor: Self-aware sense of the applicant's particular strengths and how they'd contribute constructively to collaborative studio work.

bullets: Name a genuine specific strength, research, construction, sketching, or organization
Give an example showing that strength in action
Show awareness that costume design in practice is collaborative, not a solo pursuit
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think what I'd bring most is thoroughness in research, I tend to be the person in a group project who goes and finds the primary sources everyone else missed, and I actually enjoy that part of the process rather than seeing it as a chore before the fun sketching starts. On a group project for a devised piece last year, I ended up building the shared research document that the rest of the team kept referring back to throughout rehearsals. I know construction is a weaker area for me right now, so I'd also want to learn from classmates who are stronger there, since I think the best studio work comes from people balancing each other's strengths rather than everyone being equally good at everything.

commonMistakes: Listing generic positive traits with no specific example
Presenting costume design as a purely individual pursuit
Overselling strengths with no honest acknowledgment of areas to grow
followUps: How do you usually respond when a group disagrees on a creative direction?
